title: HYBRID RACE PLAN
subtitle: Run hard. Move well. Hold output.
purpose: Twelve-week preparation for HYROX or The Hybrid Games (Solo or Doubles). Every athlete trains as an individual; Doubles-specific shared work is planned inside Race Day tools.
tagline: RUN HARD. MOVE WELL. HOLD OUTPUT.
supporting_statement: BUILD THE ENGINE. OWN THE STATIONS. RACE WITHOUT FALLING APART.

track_descriptions.BUILD: First-time racers, lower current training volume or return to structured training. Use the lower end of prescribed ranges, use run-walk where stated and reduce station volume before reducing movement standards.
track_descriptions.STANDARD: Suitable for most athletes. Use the middle of prescribed ranges and progress when pace, movement and recovery remain repeatable.
track_descriptions.PERFORMANCE: For experienced athletes with high current training tolerance. Use the upper end only when movement quality, pace and recovery remain stable.

independent_disclaimer: Produced independently by SEVEN3SEVEN. Designed for athletes preparing for HYROX or The Hybrid Games but not produced, approved or endorsed by either organiser. Always verify the latest published rulebook and athlete briefing.

training_terms: RPE — rating of perceived exertion; a subjective 0–10 scale used to guide effort.
Zone 2 — easy conversational aerobic effort, RPE 4-5.
Threshold — controlled hard running at RPE 7.5-8 that can be sustained for extended blocks.
Race-distance repetition — a running interval at the exact race run distance (1 km HYROX, 600 m Hybrid Games).
Compromised running — running immediately after a station under residual fatigue.
Brick — a session stacking running with station work in event order.
Deload — a reduced-volume week designed to absorb accumulated training.
Taper — the final phase before race day: lower volume, retain small doses of race pace and load.
No-rep — a repetition disallowed by the judge for failing the movement standard.
Transition — the change between run and station, or station and station.
movement_standards: Sled push — hips low, arms long, push through the floor. Reset if the sled stops mid-lane.
Sled pull — hand-over-hand or rope-over-shoulder. Rope management costs seconds.
Burpee broad jump — chest to floor, two-foot take-off and landing behind the line.
Wall ball — legal squat depth and ball contact above the target line.
Lunge — legal knee contact where required. Full extension at the top of each step.
Farmers carry — chest tall, controlled turns, avoid dropping the implements.
Dumbbell snatch — one clean pull from the floor to overhead. Alternate hands as prescribed.
Machine stations — practise damper, footplate and monitor setup as part of the transition.
race_guidance: Pacing principle — the second half should not be significantly slower than the first.
Station break plan — decide set sizes and breaths in advance; do not decide mid-set.
Doubles — plan A/B stations and handover cues before race day.
Fuel and hydration — practise pre-race meal, fluids and carbohydrate in rehearsals only.
Official information — always verify the latest published rulebook and athlete briefing.
equipment_substitutions: Running → treadmill at 1% incline if outdoor running is unsafe.
SkiErg → tall-kneeling banded pulls if no ergometer is available.
Rower → SkiErg or bike at equivalent RPE, matching duration not distance.
Air bike → any bike ergometer at matched effort.
Sled → heavy resistance-band drag or hill push at matched effort.
Wall balls → heavy squat-to-press with a dumbbell.
Farmers carry → dual kettlebells or trap-bar carry at matched load.
Lunges → walking lunges bodyweight or dumbbells at matched load.
Burpee broad jumps → burpee-to-target if space is limited.
Dumbbell snatch → kettlebell snatch at similar load and reps.

articles.title: Built for Hybrid Racing
articles.intro: Hybrid performance is the ability to run hard, move load, protect standards and recover enough to do it again.
key_points: Engine — running volume and aerobic capacity decide how well pace returns after stations.
Strength reserve — stronger athletes use a lower percentage of max capacity at race load.
Station density — work rate, standards and transitions decide whether fitness becomes performance.
Compromised running — the race is won by the athlete who can run well after loaded work.
Decision quality — pacing, set size and break discipline stop the race from unravelling.
articles.principle: Race principle: early restraint creates late performance. The fastest opening pace is rarely the fastest finishing strategy.

articles.title: How to Use the Plan
articles.intro: Five core sessions develop the engine, force, station economy and compromised running. The sixth session is optional recovery and skills, not another hard day.
weekly_sessions: Build force reserve and sled ability.
Develop threshold, race-distance rhythm and speed reserve.
Develop race-load movement economy and repeatability.
Practise running after station fatigue and record drop-off.
Restore, practise movement standards and support the next week.

articles.title: Intensity and Load Levels
articles.intro: The programme uses RPE for gym strength, benchmark pace for run quality and load levels for race stations.
station_load_levels: Specific phase, rehearsals and key station sessions.
Sled only, short exposures, no stalls.
race_volume_levels: Technique, taper, short exposure and confidence.
Early specific work and lower-fatigue rehearsals.
Most specific race-prep bricks and partial simulations.
Major rehearsal only; stop before form breaks.
Race day only unless directly coached.
articles.progression: Progression order: standard first, then volume, then load, then density. Do not increase all four at once.

articles.title: Pace Drop-Off and Race Pace
articles.intro: The aim is not one heroic split. The aim is repeatable speed when the legs and grip are already loaded.
tools: Drop-off % = (slowest repeat - fastest repeat) / fastest repeat x 100. Keep most quality work under 5-8% unless the session says otherwise.
Use the fastest pace you can repeat while movement standards remain legal and breathing returns before the next station.
Start slightly under target. If the first two runs feel exciting, they are probably too fast.
Use 100-200 m controlled fast efforts only when posture and breathing stay stable.
articles.principle: Seven3Seven standard: the last repeat should still look coached. If it looks like survival, the first half was too hot.

articles.title: Choosing Load and Race Volume
articles.intro: Load is how heavy the station is. Race volume is how much of the race station you complete.
decisions: Start at the written Station Load Level. Increase only when every rep is legal, posture stays strong and output repeats.
Use RVL as the station-volume cap. RVL rises across the plan, then falls during taper.
Reduce load or volume if no-reps appear, feet stop on sleds, grip fails repeatedly or the next run collapses.
Progress one variable only: standard first, then volume, then load, then density.
articles.principle: Target: zero no-reps. If no-reps appear, record them and reduce volume or load next exposure.

articles.title: Breaking Stations Without Panic
articles.intro: Good athletes plan breaks before fatigue forces them. Small planned breaks beat late uncontrolled stops.
strategies: Choose sets you can repeat without no-reps. Break before squat depth, target height or breathing fails.
Keep legal length and rhythm. Shorter legal jumps can beat long jumps that ruin the next run.
Set grip before lifting, use clean turns and avoid panic drops. Planned quick breaks are better than failed grip.
Protect posture and lockout. Break before stride length shortens or knee contact becomes inconsistent.
Feet must keep moving. If the sled stalls, the load, surface or angle is wrong for that day.
articles.principle: Race execution rule: never spend standards to buy speed. Illegal reps are not performance.

learn.safety: This programme provides educational training guidance and does not replace medical diagnosis, injury rehabilitation or individual clinical advice. Stop for sharp pain, chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual shortness of breath. Use competent coaching when learning unfamiliar movements.
